content: 1. Update the monitoring system to identify individuals who miss a scheduled clinic visit. Ensure that a follow-up call is made within one week of the missed appointment to inquire about adverse events, tuberculosis (TB) symptoms, pregnancy status, and the availability of medications. Additionally, schedule the next clinic appointment as soon as possible. 2. For interruptions in TB preventive treatment (TPT) regimens such as 3HR, 4R, or 6H: If the interruption is less than two weeks, resume treatment immediately upon return and extend the total treatment duration by the number of missed days. Address the reason for the interruption, counsel the patient and caregiver on the importance of adherence, and agree on strategies to improve adherence. If the interruption exceeds two weeks and more than 80% of the expected doses have been taken, no further action is required. Continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. If less than 80% of the doses were taken and the treatment cannot be completed within the expected timeframe, consider restarting the full TPT course. 3. For the 3HP weekly regimen: If a single dose is missed and remembered within two days, the dose can be taken immediately, and the remaining doses should follow the original schedule. If the missed dose is remembered after two days, take the missed dose immediately and adjust the weekly schedule to the new day until treatment completion. Ensure that no two weekly doses are taken less than four days apart. If more than one weekly dose is missed: For 1–3 missed doses, continue treatment until all 12 doses are completed, extending the treatment duration to a maximum of 16 weeks. For four or more missed doses, consider restarting the full TPT course. If adherence to a weekly routine is not feasible, discontinue 3HP and offer an alternative daily regimen. 4. For the 1HP regimen: If less than one week of doses is missed and more than 80% of the expected doses (23 doses) have been taken, no action is required. Complete the remaining doses. If less than 80% of the doses were taken, resume treatment immediately upon return and extend the total treatment duration to complete the course within a maximum of six weeks. If more than one week of doses is missed: For seven consecutive missed doses, consider restarting the full 1HP course. For intermittent missed doses exceeding seven, resume treatment immediately and extend the total treatment duration to complete the course within a maximum of eight weeks. If adherence to 1HP is not possible, discontinue it and offer an alternative daily regimen or 3HP. 5. Governments and donors should support systematic monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of TPT programmatic management to generate strategic information. Investment in digital solutions for recording and reporting TPT services is essential. 6. M&E plays a critical role in patient care and assessing national programs and global responses. Accurate data recording and reporting provide insights into program outputs, outcomes, and the impact of resources invested. M&E should inform healthcare providers and program managers about the effectiveness of contact investigations, TPT initiation, and completion rates. 7. Monitoring programmatic implementation of TPT requires strengthening each element of the care cascade, from identifying the target population to providing and continuing TPT. Critical numbers to monitor include the number of individuals eligible for TPT, those evaluated for eligibility, those who started TPT, and those who completed it. 8. Indicators for monitoring TPT include: Contact investigation coverage: The percentage of contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients evaluated for TB disease and infection. TPT initiation: The percentage of eligible individuals who started TPT during the reporting period. TPT completion: The percentage of individuals completing TPT out of those who initiated treatment. 9. Ministries of health and national programs should integrate TPT M&E into existing health management information systems (HMIS). Establishing a parallel data collection system for TPT is neither required nor desirable. 10. A minimum individual-level dataset for TPT monitoring should include: Assessment of TB patient contacts: Contact identifier, demographics, TB screening results, eligibility determination date, and decision to prescribe TPT. Assessment of people living with HIV (PLHIV) and other at-risk groups: Risk group identifier, demographics, TB screening results, eligibility determination date, and decision to prescribe TPT. TPT initiation and completion: Person identifier, prescribed regimen, initiation date, and completion date. 11. Programmatic barriers, such as medication adherence and adverse drug reactions, should be reviewed. If routine pharmacovigilance systems are inadequate, data on adverse drug reactions (frequency, organ class, severity, and seriousness) should be collected.
